For public safety and comfort, a minimum of three lean-to style shelters would be constructed initially at yet undetermined sites along the proposed trail. Each shelter would accommodate approximately six persons and their gear. The shelters should be spaced to provide the maximum benefit for hikers, and located away from major highway access points to avoid conflicts in public use. In addition, each shelter should be located near a potable water source, such as a spring, stream, or lake. The proposed trail should have appropriate signs and blazes to clearly identify the trail route and indicate mileage distances, the location of shelters, and rules of conduct. Annual vegetative clearing should be undertaken as needed to maintain the trail as a readily recognizable route and thus reduce the risk of people getting lost or injured. Each trail access point at a highway crossing, such as at Highway 178, should have limited space available for adjacent off-road parking to insure public safety. Appropriate public crossings should be provided at streams along the trail route, including the Thompson and Horsepasture Rivers. These recommended measures are further discussed in Section 9 herein.
The proposed hiking trail would closely interrelate with Forest Service management of the Whitewater River Unit (see Subsection 3.1.1.1 herein). The proposed project recreation plan appears to be fully compatible with the Forest Service plan.
The level of public use anticipated along the proposed hiking trail would not have a significant impact at its eastern terminus, Table Rock State Park. Existing facilities at the park should adequately accommodate a slight increase in visitation.
Operation of the proposed Bad Creek Reservoir would have a slight stabilizing effect of fluctuations of Lake Jocassee. This would enhance the recreational attractiveness of that lake to a limited extent. Public safety hazards near the proposed Bad Creek discharge structure on Lake Jocassee would be minimized through provision of appropriate warning devices to indicate when operations are about to begin, including flashing lights and warning horns, as well as signs.
